lines.say: Claude can read and write your code. But can it open your website, and click the buttons, like a real user?
Out of the box, no. In this video, you'll give it that power, with MCP.
I'll explain what MCP is, when to use it, and then we'll connect a real server together, step by step.

scenes.heading: What is [[MCP]]?
items: **Model Context Protocol**: an open standard that connects AI to tools and data
An **MCP server** gives Claude new tools: a browser, GitHub, your database…
Add a server once, and Claude **uses its tools when they help**

card.title: ONE STANDARD, MANY TOOLS
card.code:
Claude Code
  │  MCP
  ├─ playwright → a real browser
  ├─ github     → issues, pull requests
  └─ database   → your data

lines.say: So, what is MCP?
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It's an open standard for connecting AI to tools and data.
Think of it like a USB-C port for AI. One standard plug, and many different tools can connect to it.
Each connection is called an MCP server. A server gives Claude new tools, like a web browser, GitHub, or your database.
You add a server once, and from then on, Claude uses its tools whenever they help.

scenes.heading: How MCP [[works]]

rows.label: Claude Code connects
rows.text: The server tells Claude which tools it offers

rows.label: Claude uses the tools
rows.text: It calls them when they help, and reads the results

scenes.banner: ✓ Local servers run on your computer · remote servers live at a URL

lines.say: Here's how it works, in three parts.
First, you add a server, with one command: claude mcp add.
Second, when a session starts, Claude Code connects to the server, and the server lists the tools it offers.
Third, Claude calls those tools when they help with your request, and the results come back into the conversation.
Some servers run locally on your computer. Others are hosted online, at a URL.

left.title: Without MCP
left.body:
You copy data into the chat

• Paste error logs, issues, query results
• Claude only sees what you paste
• Slow, and easy to miss things

right.title: With MCP
right.body:
Claude reads and acts on the tool directly

• Opens the page, reads the issue
• Always the real, current data
• You just ask

lines.say: So when should you use MCP?
Here's a simple rule. If you keep copying data from another tool into the chat, like error logs, issues, or query results, that's a sign.
Connect that tool with MCP instead, and Claude can read and act on it directly, with the real, current data.

left.title: index.html · a newsletter signup form
left.code: Thanks! Check your inbox.

right.title: With the Playwright MCP server
right.body:
Claude opens the page in Chrome
→ types an email, clicks the button
→ sees what a real user sees
→ finds the bug, and fixes it

lines.say: Our example: letting Claude test a website, like a real user.
Here's a small newsletter page with a signup form. When you sign up, a thank-you message should appear.
With the Playwright MCP server, Claude can open the page in Chrome, fill in the form, click the button, and check what really happens.
First, the problem. Here's my page. I start Claude Code, and ask it to check the signup in a browser.

do.text:
Get free AI tools every week

Thanks! Check your inbox.

lines.say: Open my page in a browser, and check that signing up works.

do.text: Open my page in a browser and check that signing up works

lines.say: Claude can read my code, but it can't open a browser, or click buttons. So I'd have to test it by hand.

lines: ai:I can read index.html, but I can't open a browser or click buttons, so I can't test the signup the way a user would. You could test it manually, or I can review the code.

lines.say: Let's give Claude a real browser.
Step one: find a server.
There are hundreds of MCP servers. A good place to look is the Anthropic Directory, or the docs of the tool you use.
For our example, I pick Playwright, from Microsoft. It gives Claude a real browser, and it needs no account. Just Node.js, version 18 or later.
Step two: add it.
In my terminal, not inside Claude, I run claude mcp add, a name I choose, playwright, then two dashes, and the command that starts the server.

out: Added stdio MCP server playwright with command:

lines.say: The two dashes matter. Everything after them is the command Claude Code runs to start the server.
The confirmation says local config. That means the server is just for me, in this project.
Step three: check that it connects.
I run claude mcp list.
Connected means it's ready. The very first check can fail while the package downloads, so just wait a moment, and run it again.
Step four: use it.
First, I serve my page locally, with Python's built-in web server.
Then, in a second terminal, I start Claude, and ask it to test the signup with playwright.

do.text: Use playwright to open http://localhost:8000, sign up with test@example.com, and tell me what happens

lines.say: A Chrome window opens, so you can watch it work. Notice each tool call is labeled with the server name, playwright, and the action.
If Claude Code asks for permission the first time, approve it.
Claude checks the page, and the console, and finds the real bug: the thank-you message never appears.

lines: res:TypeError: Cannot set properties of null
ai:Found a bug: after clicking Sign up, the thank-you message never appears. The script looks for id "sucess", but the message's id is "success".

do.label: What a real user would see

lines.say: It's a one-letter typo. Easy to miss when you read the code, but obvious in a real browser.
I ask Claude to fix it, and test it again.

do.text:
Get free AI tools every week

Thanks! Check your inbox.

lines.say: This time, the message appears. Claude didn't just read my code. It used my page, like a real user.

lines: ai:Fixed and re-tested: "Thanks! Check your inbox." now appears, and there are no console errors.

cards.title: Share with your team
cards.text: Add `--scope project` to save it in `.mcp.json`

cards.title: Only trust servers you know
cards.text: A server can run code and see your data

cards.title: Remove what you don't use
cards.text: Each server takes space in Claude's context

lines.say: Step five: go further. Here are four tips.
One: add dash dash scope project, and the server is saved in a dot mcp dot json file. Commit it, and your whole team gets the same tools.
Two: type slash mcp inside Claude, or run claude mcp list, to check your servers anytime.
Three: only add servers you trust. A server can run code on your machine, and see the data you send it.
Four: remove servers you don't use, with claude mcp remove. Each connected server takes some space in Claude's context window.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: MCP = a standard way to plug tools into Claude
Add a server with `claude mcp add`, check it with `claude mcp list`
Use MCP when you keep [[copying data]] into the chat

lines.say: Let's recap.
MCP is a standard way to plug tools into Claude, like a USB-C port for AI.
You add a server with claude mcp add, and check it with claude mcp list.
And whenever you keep copying data into the chat, that's your sign to connect the tool with MCP.
